summary: A tool that helps students investigate trends in NASA Earth data: pick a variable and a region, generate the time series, and test whether the change is statistically significant (regression, Mann-Kendall), including climate extremes such as drought, heavy rain, and fire-prone conditions.
details:
Earth Data Detective turns trend analysis of Earth science data into a guided investigation. Users choose a variable (temperature, precipitation, humidity, solar radiation, wind, or a livestock heat-stress index) and a region (major crop and cattle-producing areas, cities, or custom coordinates). The app retrieves the monthly time series, removes the seasonal cycle, plots the evolution over time, and computes the rate of change with a confidence interval, a t-test, the Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope, and the Hamed-Rao test, which corrects for autocorrelation. The result is a plain-language verdict: significant trend, mixed result, or no significant trend.

A second tab analyzes climate extremes (heavy-rain days, dry spells, extreme heat, strong wind, and fire-prone conditions) from daily data, then checks whether they follow the drought or rainfall of previous months using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and lagged correlation. A companion web tool accepts time series from Giovanni and AppEEARS for variables such as NDVI, ozone, and soil moisture.

How we addressed the challenge
We cover all four elements of the challenge: selecting variables with simple definitions, acquiring data for a specific region, visualizing time series, and performing statistical analysis of the rate of change and its significance. We also followed the suggested considerations: demonstration regions (deforestation, agriculture, livestock, the Arctic), warnings about short records, and the idea that a non-significant trend is still informative and may become significant with a longer record.

How we built it
Python, Streamlit, pandas, SciPy, Plotly, and pymannkendall for the app; HTML and JavaScript for the companion web tool. Code and documentation are in the project README.

NASA data and resources used
NASA POWER (derived from MERRA-2 and GPM), with Giovanni, AppEEARS, and Hydrology Time Series as sources for additional variables. The SeaWiFS time-series article and trend-testing guides informed our methodology.

Use of artificial intelligence
Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, was used to support solution design, code writing, and documentation. Space Apps asks for transparency about AI use, so check the exact field in the form and adjust this text to reflect what your team actually did and reviewed.
